What this course is

A practical 20-hour programme that takes you from the basics of money laundering to writing a strong STR and running an AML function. Every part links to how real cases are built in Pakistan.

📚

Complete coverage

AML, CFT, proliferation financing, KYC, monitoring, STR, MLRO duties and bank financial crimes.

🔍

Investigator's view

You see how cases are traced, frozen and prosecuted, not only how rules are written.

🇵🇰

Built for Pakistan

AML Act, SBP and SECP rules, FMU and goAML, plus FATF standards used worldwide.

📁

Toolkit included

Templates, presentations and sample cases you can reuse at work, from STR formats to risk assessment sheets.

⏱

On demand

No fixed batch. Start when you are ready and finish at your own speed.

🎓

Certificate

Pass the final test and receive a certificate issued by the hosting portal and signed by the instructor.

Who can attend

  • Students of ACCA, CA, CIMA, ICMA, PIPFA, MBA Finance, BBA Finance and related fields
  • Bankers and compliance staff, including AML, KYC and branch teams
  • Government officials who deal with financial crime, tax or regulation
  • Auditors, lawyers, fintech and crypto staff, and DNFBP teams
  • Anyone moving into compliance or financial investigation

Eligibility

  • No licence or prior AML work needed
  • Basic understanding of banking or accounts helps
  • Comfortable with English or Urdu
  • A laptop or phone and a steady connection
  • About 4 to 6 weeks at 4 to 5 hours a week suits most people

Why this matters for Pakistan, right now

🇵🇰

National standing

The 2018 to 2022 grey list years showed what weak controls cost: harder banking, slower investment and lost trust. Staying out is a daily job, not a one-time win.

💰

Economy and remittances

Remittances, exports and IMF and World Bank support all depend on a financial system the world trusts.

⚠

New risks

Crypto, digital wallets and trade-based laundering are growing faster than the number of trained people.

🛡

Security

Stopping terror and proliferation financing protects lives, not only balance sheets.

In the national interest: every STR filed on time and every case built properly supports the country's standing. Trained professionals in banks, firms and agencies are how that standing is kept.

Needed beyond borders too

One global standard

FATF rules are the same in the Gulf, UK, Europe, Asia and North America, so your skill moves with you.

Cross-border crime

Hawala, trade fraud and online scams cross borders, so every country needs people who can read the trail.

Global hiring

Banks, exchange houses and fintechs abroad keep hiring AML staff, including remote roles.

Why AML matters

Dirty money hurts banks, businesses and the country. Regulators now expect trained people in every institution, and that expectation is not going away.

Six reasons to care

Tap any card for the short version.

Pakistan's road so far

2010
AML Act passed, creating the Financial Monitoring Unit and STR reporting.
2018
FATF places Pakistan on its grey list, starting years of reform pressure.
2020
Second Amendment to the AML Act brings stronger investigation, confiscation and penalty powers.
2022
Pakistan exits the FATF grey list after completing its action plans.
2023
National Risk Assessment refreshed to guide banks, regulators and agencies.
2026
Virtual Assets Act and the regulator PVARA bring crypto into the AML net. Trade-based laundering is a growing focus.

Leaving a list is not the end. Mutual evaluations and follow-ups continue, so institutions need people who can keep standards up every year.

Numbers worth knowing

Trade-based laundering

A 31 August 2026 report on TBML cites a 398% surge and flagged values of about Rs 3.4 trillion (around $21bn), as reported.

Penalties

The AML Act carries prison terms and heavy fines for laundering and for failing to report suspicious activity.

Who must comply

Banks, DFIs, exchange companies, securities and insurance firms, and DNFBPs such as accountants and real estate.

Careers and jobs

AML skills travel. The same knowledge applies in a Karachi bank, a Dubai exchange house or a remote compliance desk for a fintech.

Market worth

Steady demand

Every regulated firm needs compliance staff, and rules keep widening to cover crypto, fintech, real estate and accountants.

Scarce skill

Many finance graduates know accounting but few can draft an STR or defend a risk assessment. That gap is where you stand out.

Global currency

FATF standards are the same worldwide, so your learning supports roles in the Gulf, UK and beyond.

Pay

Salaries vary by city, firm and seniority. Check live listings before you plan. Compliance roles usually pay above general operations roles at the same level.

Where to look

  • Banks and DFIs: AML, KYC, sanctions and fraud units
  • Exchange companies, payment firms and fintechs
  • Big four and consulting firms: forensic and risk advisory
  • Regulators and agencies: SBP, SECP, FMU, FIA, FBR, NAB
  • Gulf and UK institutions, including remote compliance and screening roles
  • Training and consulting on your own once you have experience

Syeda Alisha Imran

Sub Inspector, FIA Former Investigation Officer, AML Circle Karachi ACCA

Alisha joined the Federal Investigation Agency in 2022 as a Sub Inspector and worked as an Investigation Officer in the AML Circle, Karachi. She handled money laundering, bank fraud and economic crime cases. She is ACCA qualified and holds a Bachelor of Commerce from the University of Karachi.

Her work covered financial investigation, cybercrime analysis, evidence handling, raids and working with other agencies, including requests for international assistance. She trained on the AML Act through a US embassy programme and on mutual legal assistance for terror financing cases with UNODC.

In this course she teaches the way she worked: start from the money trail, build the file, and write it so it holds up.

Questions people ask

Already ACCA, CA, CIMA, MBA or BBA Finance qualified? You can still take this course and move into this field, just as Alisha did after her ACCA.

The AML Practitioner Programme is educational training. It is not legal advice and does not replace regulator guidance or external exams. Laws and thresholds change, so always confirm current rules. Case examples are taught for learning and do not comment on cases still before the courts.
